confidence_note: The Petrified Forest National Park field study is Cialdini's own research and is reported in later editions of Influence; the 1984 first edition year is as given by the catalogue. Checked against secondary summaries only. The size of the effect is kept to 'nearly three times the no-sign level' (secondary summaries disagree on exact percentages, 7.92 and 2.92 and 1.67 were seen); percentages, tonnage figures and exact sign wording are omitted. The 'please do not remove' sign is described only as a plain request.
facts: Petrified Forest National Park in Arizona had a problem with visitors taking pieces of petrified wood.
A natural response was a sign telling visitors that many people already take wood from the park.
Cialdini and colleagues tested sign messages in the park: they placed secretly marked pieces of petrified wood along visitor paths and counted how many disappeared.
The sign saying many past visitors took wood, with a picture of several people taking pieces, led to theft rising to nearly three times the level on a path with no sign.
A sign that simply asked visitors not to remove the wood did better, with fewer pieces vanishing.
Cialdini's reading: a warning that stresses how common a bad behaviour is can make it look normal, so the message works against its own aim.
He calls this negative social proof.
Cialdini reads messages as doing one of two jobs: showing what others actually do, or saying what should be done. The sign did the first; the plain request the second.
scene_details: secretly marked pieces of petrified wood along visitor paths
a sign with a picture of several people taking pieces of wood
a plain sign asking visitors not to remove wood
tension: A park posts a warning against theft and the theft rises.
opening_idea: Open on the marked pieces of wood lying on the paths and the count of how many vanished under each sign.

lessons.idea: When you want to stop a behaviour, do not tell people how many others do it; say what you want them to do.
lessons.anchor: the sign that stressed how many visitors took wood

reflect_final: When did you last explain a rule by saying how many people break it, and how could you word it by saying what you want instead?

use_cases.situation: You write a reminder to the team about late timesheets.
use_cases.move: Skip 'many of you are late'; state the deadline and what you want done.

use_cases.situation: You tell your teenager that everyone leaves dishes in the sink.
use_cases.move: Drop the 'everyone does' line and ask for the dishes in the dishwasher after dinner.

use_cases.situation: A friend complains that a group chat is full of skipped payments.
use_cases.move: Mention the Petrified Forest sign, and suggest saying 'please pay by Friday' instead of listing who has not.

pocket_idea: A park's warning that many visitors took wood led to more theft; name the behaviour you want, not the one that is common.

conversation_variants.punchline_idea: A sign in a national park saying many people take petrified wood led visitors to take nearly three times as much.
conversation_variants.thirty_sec_idea: A park in Arizona wanted visitors to stop taking petrified wood, so it told them many others did. Cialdini's team marked pieces and counted: more went missing than on a path with no sign. A plain request not to take any worked better.
